steps.title: Prepare computer hardware
steps.instruction: Allocate a workstation (≈2 min) with at least an Intel® Core™ i7‑10700K CPU, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU, 32 GB DDR4 RAM, 1 TB SSD, running Windows 11; note that any comparable multi‑core CPU, GPU, memory and storage configuration is acceptable.

steps.title: Install Python environment
steps.instruction: Set up the software foundation by installing Anaconda, then install PyTorch and create an isolated Python virtual environment for this protocol.

substeps.instruction: Download and install Anaconda.
Install PyTorch within the Anaconda environment.
Create a new Python virtual environment (e.g., `conda create -n sers_env python=3.9`).

steps.title: Install required packages
steps.instruction: Within the activated virtual environment, install the essential Python libraries via pip.

substeps.instruction: pip install numpy
pip install matplotlib
pip install pandas
pip install seaborn

steps.title: Preprocess Raman spectra
steps.instruction: Transform raw SERS spectra into a 2‑D image representation ready for deep‑learning analysis.

substeps.instruction: Apply Savitzky‑Golay smoothing: `y_filter = savgol_filter(y, 21, 5, mode="nearest")` (window = 21, polynomial order = 5).
Perform morphology‑based iterative baseline correction: `y_baseline_correction = y_uniform - y_baseline`.
Define Raman shift as X‑axis and intensity as Y‑axis; map each data point one‑to‑one.
Resample the spectra with linear interpolation to obtain evenly spaced points.
Connect interpolated points with a solid line to generate a continuous spectral curve.
Interpret the resulting curve as a spatial intensity map over the Raman‑shift range.
Save each map as an image of size 328 × 328 px (MATLAB command: `set(gcf,'Position',[0,0,328,328])`), naming files as `AL-<i+4284>.png`.

steps.title: Extract and fuse features
steps.instruction: Derive complementary 1‑D and 2‑D feature vectors and combine them for classification.

substeps.instruction: Run PCA on the pre‑processed 1‑D spectra with `n_components=1024`; ensure cumulative variance > 95%:
```python
pca = PCA(n_components=1024)
pca.fit(y_uniform)
low_d = pca.transform(y_uniform)
low_d = low_d.reshape((2888, 1, 1024)).astype('float64')
variances = pca.explained_variance_ratio_ * 100
cumulative_variances = np.cumsum(variances)
Crop each 2‑D spectral image to the central 224 × 224 px region to satisfy ResNet50 input requirements.
Feed the cropped images into a pre‑trained ResNet50 model and extract high‑level image features (`data_npy`).
Concatenate the PCA‑derived 1‑D features (`low_d`) with the ResNet50 image features:
```python
e = np.concatenate((low_d, data_npy), axis=2)
classdata = np.concatenate((e, label), axis=2)

steps.title: Build Transformer classifier
steps.instruction: Construct a Transformer‑based model that consumes the fused feature vectors and outputs class probabilities.

substeps.instruction: Define six classification categories (e.g., normal vs. leukemia, AML vs. ALL, B‑ALL vs. T‑ALL).
Create an embedding layer: `self.embedding = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)`. Feed fused features into this layer.
Generate Q, K, V vectors via separate linear projections.
Compute attention scores: `scores = torch.matmul(q, k.permute(0,1,3,2))` and apply softmax.
Apply attention weights to V, add dropout (rate = 0.1) and layer‑norm:
```python
attn_weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
attended_vals = torch.matmul(attn_weights, v)
attended_vals = self.norm1(attended_vals)
attended_vals = self.dropout(attended_vals)
Pass the result through a linear output layer: `output = self.fco(attended_vals)`.
Perform adaptive average pooling to reduce dimensionality: `self.pooling = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1)`.
MLP block: two linear layers with ReLU activation and dropout = 0.1 after each.
Final fully‑connected layer to map to `output_dim`:
```python
self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, output_dim)
For binary tasks apply Sigmoid (`self.sigmoid = nn.Sigmoid()`); for multi‑class tasks apply Softmax.
Set loss functions: `criterion = nn.BCELoss()` for binary, `criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()` for multi‑class.
Configure optimizer: `optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.0001)` with batch size = 2.

steps.title: Train and select model
steps.instruction: Fit the Transformer model to the data, monitor validation performance, and retain the best‑performing weights.

substeps.instruction: Split the dataset into training, validation, and test sets in an 8:1:1 ratio.
Train for 300 epochs, updating parameters each batch (size = 2) with learning rate = 0.0001.
During training, compute validation accuracy after each epoch.
Save the model checkpoint that achieves the highest validation accuracy and use it for final testing.

description: Central nervous system leukemia (CNSL) is a significant contributor to leukemia relapse and drug resistance, and may lead to severe complications or life-threatening conditions. Therefore, prompt identification of affected patients and timely administration of symptomatic treatment are critical.2,3 Currently, clinical diagnosis primarily relies on neurological symptom evaluation, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and neuroimaging studies. Among these methods, conventional cytology (CC) examination of CSF is considered the gold standard for confirming central nervous system involvement.4 However, its sensitivity is relatively low (<50%), often resulting in false-negative results, despite a specificity greater than 95%.5,6 Moreover, biomarkers released into the CSF by leukemic cells enable a diagnostic approach that is more sensitive, accurate, and quantifiable than traditional cytological techniques.2 These biomarkers can reflect key biological processes such as leukemic cell migration and adhesion to the central nervous system, metabolic plasticity, and intercellular interactions. As a result, biomarker-based detection and diagnosis of CNSL using CSF samples are increasingly becoming a focal point in current research.7 Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) is a molecular fingerprinting spectroscopic technique that offers high sensitivity, excellent specificity, rapid detection capability, suitability for in situ analysis, and the ability to simultaneously recognize multiple components, making it particularly advantageous in diverse analytical applications.8,9 The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly accelerated the development and application of SERS technology.
